lead: QR decomposition writes a matrix A as Q times R. Q has orthonormal columns. R is upper triangular. The columns of Q come from running Gram–Schmidt on the columns of A. R stores the numbers used in that run. It exists so that least-squares problems and repeated solves can avoid forming AᵀA. Numerical libraries use it for regression, signal fitting and computer graphics. Only a few universities teach this chapter.

blocks.text: Take A with columns a₁,…,aₙ in ℝᵐ. Run Gram–Schmidt from 5.4. At step j, subtract from aⱼ its parts along q₁,…,qⱼ₋₁: vⱼ = aⱼ − Σᵢ₌₁ʲ⁻¹ ⟨aⱼ,qᵢ⟩ qᵢ. Then qⱼ = vⱼ/‖vⱼ‖. The numbers subtracted at step j are the off-diagonal entries rᵢⱼ = ⟨aⱼ, qᵢ⟩ for i < j. The diagonal entry rⱼⱼ = ‖vⱼ‖ is the length used to normalise, not a number subtracted.

For i > j set rᵢⱼ = 0. Diagonal entries are positive because vⱼ ≠ 0 when columns are independent. The thin form has Q m×n and R n×n. The full form adds m−n extra orthonormal columns to Q and zero rows below R.
A = QR,   rᵢⱼ = ⟨aⱼ, qᵢ⟩ (i < j),   rⱼⱼ = ‖vⱼ‖ > 0
blocks.where: A is m×n with independent columns; Q is m×n with orthonormal columns; R is n×n upper triangular; aⱼ is column j of A; qᵢ is column i of Q; vⱼ is the Gram–Schmidt vector before normalising.

blocks.text: Because QᵀQ = I, AᵀA = (QR)ᵀ(QR) = RᵀQᵀQR = RᵀR. The normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb from 5.5 become RᵀRx = RᵀQᵀb. Cancel Rᵀ when R is invertible: Rx = Qᵀb. R is upper triangular, so solve by back substitution. This avoids forming AᵀA, which can square the condition number and lose accuracy.

blocks.where: x is the least-squares solution; R is n×n upper triangular; Qᵀb is n×1; b is the m×1 data vector.

blocks.text: A QR least-squares solve is two steps: form y = Qᵀb, then back-substitute Rx = y. The residual is ‖Ax − b‖. When columns are independent, R is invertible. If columns are dependent, R has a zero on the diagonal and thin QR with positive diagonal does not exist. In practice, Qᵀb is one matrix-vector product. Back substitution costs about n²/2 operations.

figure.caption: Gram–Schmidt on the two columns of A produces Q and the upper triangular R; the same factors turn a least-squares problem into a triangular solve.

spec.title: QR from Gram–Schmidt
spec.aria: A flow from the columns of A through Gram–Schmidt to the factors Q and R, and then to solving a triangular system.

examples.question: Find the thin QR decomposition of A = [[1,1],[1,0],[0,1]] and check that A = QR.
examples.answer: A = QR with Q = [q₁ q₂] and R = [[√2, 1/√2],[0, √6/2]], so the thin QR decomposition is A = QR.
examples.check:
import math
a1 = [1,1,0]
a2 = [1,0,1]
n1 = math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in a1))
q1 = [x/n1 for x in a1]
r12 = sum(a2[i]*q1[i] for i in range(3))
v2 = [a2[i] - r12*q1[i] for i in range(3)]
n2 = math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in v2))
print(n1)
print(r12)
print(n2)

traps: Filling only the diagonal of R with norms and forgetting off-diagonal rᵢⱼ = ⟨aⱼ,qᵢ⟩; then QR cannot rebuild A.
Using aᵢ instead of qᵢ in rᵢⱼ = ⟨aⱼ,qᵢ⟩; the second vector must be the orthonormal one.
Writing A = RQ or Q = AR; the triangular factor multiplies on the right.

Sign slip: qⱼ can be multiplied by −1, but then row j of R must also change sign (rⱼⱼ becomes negative). A = QR = Σᵢ qᵢ · (row i of R). The usual convention rⱼⱼ > 0 removes the choice. Always check the full product A = QR, not just matching columns of Q on their own.
For least squares, solving RᵀRx = Qᵀb instead of cancelling to Rx = Qᵀb; cancel only when R is invertible.

quiz.q: What property do the columns of Q have in thin QR?

quiz.a: aⱼ lies in span{q₁,…,qⱼ}, so ⟨aⱼ, qᵢ⟩ = 0 for every i > j. Hence rᵢⱼ = 0 for i > j: column j of R has zeros below the diagonal, so R is upper triangular.

quiz.q: For A = [[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]], find q₁ and r₁₂.
Solve Rx = Qᵀb for R = [[2,1],[0,3]], Qᵀb = (4,9).
A has dependent columns. What fails in thin QR?
quiz.a: Some vⱼ=0, so rⱼⱼ=0; R is singular and positive diagonal cannot be kept.

quiz.q: Why is QR preferred over normal equations for least squares?
quiz.a: AᵀA squares the condition number; QR keeps Q orthogonal and R triangular, so it is more stable.

beyond: Not for the exam. QR is the workhorse behind numpy.linalg.qr, MATLAB's qr and LAPACK's Householder routines. Search for Householder QR, modified Gram–Schmidt, and QR least squares in regression. In graphics, QR helps orthonormalise animation frames.
